Start with the fastest agent pilot and use its usage data to define the other groups’ needs afterward.
Assign an acceptance owner to each requirement and resolve speed-versus-reviewability conflicts before selecting a solution.

prompt: A discovery workshop produces a list of desired features, but no requirement is linked to an affected user, workflow observation, acceptance measure, or accountable owner. The sponsor asks for architecture selection immediately. Select TWO: Which discovery outputs should precede architecture selection?

constraints: The discovery traceability matrix, interview coverage, workflow observations, authority decisions, acceptance measures, unresolved-question log, and lifecycle owner are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a high-impact role, authority decision, or acceptance measure were still missing, discovery would remain open and the existing scoped-discovery path would apply.
details.errorCorrection: The first has no evidence boundary and adds noise; the second loses the completed authority and acceptance record that should govern design. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends defining measurable, use-case-relevant criteria before iterating on prompts or implementation. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a revisit trigger, hand the bounded requirements to design, and reopen only if new evidence crosses the trigger.
details.transfer: Close a discovery phase with evidence, ownership, residual uncertainty, and a trigger that tells the team when to reopen it.

messages.text: Collecting more suggestions before setting an exit boundary adds noise once representative requirements and acceptance evidence are complete.
An undocumented handoff loses the authority and acceptance record that should govern design.
Indefinite discovery has no owner-controlled exit and delays design without changing the authorized brief.

feedback.reason: Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a revisit trigger, hand the bounded requirements to design, and reopen only if new evidence crosses the trigger. The decisive constraint is Once representative requirements and acceptance evidence are complete, discovery needs an owned exit decision; indefinite collection adds noise and delays design without changing the authorized problem brief.

options.text: Continue interviews to collect additional suggestions before setting an evidence boundary or handing requirements to design.
Move to design immediately without recording that discovery is complete or preserving the unresolved-question log.
Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a trigger, hand requirements to design, and reopen only on new evidence.
Keep discovery open indefinitely so future suggestions cannot be rejected as late.

prompt: Discovery has covered each affected role, observed the current workflow, resolved authority, and produced measurable acceptance criteria. New interview requests repeat already answered questions, and no high-impact unresolved requirement remains, but the team keeps discovery open without an exit decision. What should the team do now that discovery evidence is complete?

constraints: The current workflow and exceptions can be observed.
Backlog reduction needs a measurable outcome.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If users, workflow, target, and access rules were already documented and only a model migration remained, a solution comparison could be next.
details.errorCorrection: Model ranking and a future-state diagram assume a solution, while a field list omits workflow ownership and success evidence; a post-demo definition is too late.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic advises defining success criteria before prompt iteration and tying them to the application’s actual user needs; the problem brief structure is scenario reasoning.
details.scenarioApplication: Document each group’s advising decision, current exception path, protected records, backlog measure, and acceptance test before comparing models or architectures.
details.transfer: Resolve the problem, users, workflow, data boundary, and acceptance measure before choosing an AI solution.

messages.text: A one-group pilot can supply evidence, but it leaves the other groups’ needs and exceptions unresolved before solution selection.
Mapping fields and steps without agreed outcomes lets the agent define acceptance during the pilot instead of clarifying the problem first.
A benchmark-led choice tests capability before the university has established its own workflow, exception, and backlog evidence.

feedback.reason: The problem is still underspecified, so discovery must connect user groups and workflow evidence to the outcome, data boundary, and measurable acceptance before solution choice.

options.text: Start with one user group, pilot its current workflow, and use backlog and privacy results to shape requirements for the other groups.
Map the email and spreadsheet steps plus protected fields, then choose an agent whose pilot will discover user-group acceptance.
Write a structured problem brief connecting each user group and workflow evidence to outcome, access, data, and acceptance criteria.
Compare public advising benchmarks and choose a model, then validate exceptions and backlog measurement against the selected design.

prompt: A university asks to make advising better. Three user groups, an email and spreadsheet workflow, protected records, and a backlog-reduction target are known. What should the architect produce before selecting a solution?

constraints: Public users and owners differ from the internal audience.
Accessibility, privacy, and peak capacity changed.
The internal speed measure is not sufficient evidence.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the public portal had identical users, context, accessibility needs, and traffic contract, existing discovery evidence could carry forward.
details.errorCorrection: Scaling one latency number, copying content, or waiting for tickets does not test external usability or protect employee-only data.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic treats task fidelity, privacy preservation, context utilization, and latency as use-case-specific dimensions measured against actual needs.
details.scenarioApplication: Revisit public user tasks, screen-reader outcomes, employee-note access, peak load, escalation, and service thresholds before selecting the rollout design.
details.transfer: When context or audience changes, reopen discovery for the changed users, data boundaries, and operating envelope.

messages.text: Scaling an internal target does not establish public accessibility, privacy, or the new workflow’s owner.
Labels and a support contact do not replace discovery of public tasks or protect employee notes under the new path.
Internal criteria plus post-launch tickets leave the public accessibility and privacy boundary untested.

feedback.reason: The audience, data, accessibility, and traffic envelope changed, so inherited internal assumptions cannot establish external acceptance.

options.text: Scale the internal latency target for peak traffic, retain internal tasks, and schedule an accessibility audit after the public release.
Publish the copied FAQ with data labels and a support contact, then measure public accessibility and peak load in production.
Keep internal criteria for the first release, add a disclaimer, and route accessibility issues to support while traffic is observed.
Re-interview public users and owners, map changed data and accessibility, model peak load, and define privacy, escalation, and service criteria.

prompt: An internal FAQ assistant is moving to a public portal with non-native speakers, screen-reader users, tenfold peak traffic, and employee-only notes that must stay private. What discovery step is required?
